name: Nora Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm Ridge Farm with my dad. We've got 400 ewes, 30 beef cows, and we grow oats, turnips and hay for the winter. I'm up at six, round the sheep on the quad bike with the dogs, Bess and Moss, then the cattle, then whatever needs doing, walls, hay, the vet. Dad's knee is bad now, so most of the walking is mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the hill in the morning and knowing my great-grandfather walked it. What wears me out is the forms and the prices. Lamb prices go up and down like a yo-yo, and the government changes the rules every two years. I don't use computers more than I have to, and I've never touched one of those AI things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's a relief. I never trusted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad common sense won. You can't farm a hill from a screen, and I'd say that at church or the mart to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix our worries. Lamb prices, Dad's knee and paying for the wedding are what I think about. Callum and I are getting married next August, and every penny counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep farming the way we do. Keep putting a bit by each month, we've got about three months of bills. Go ahead with the wedding at St Michael's, keep it modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, with the usual worries in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your dad's knee gets worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm doing it all, and we'd need someone part-time at lambing. We'd ask my cousin Ewan first. Family before strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try any of the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The man at the mart tried selling me some app for my sheep records, and I said I've got a notebook and a pencil, thank you.

say: I'd say **common sense won**; you can't farm a hill from a screen.
I'd tell people at **church and the mart** the same.
think: The real worries are **lamb prices** and Dad's bad knee.
Paying for the **August wedding** means every penny counts.
do: Keep farming Ridge Farm **the way we do**.
Keep putting a bit by on top of **three months** of savings.
Hold a **modest wedding** at St Michael's next August.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, with the **usual worries** behind it.
S0.quote: The man at the mart tried selling me some app for my sheep records, and I said I've got a notebook and a pencil, thank you.
fieldNote: Her pressures are **old ones**: prices, a parent's health, a wedding.
She turns to **family first** for help, not outside workers.
Her refusal of AI is **proud** and deliberate.

steps.text: Keep running 400 ewes and 30 cows at Ridge Farm
Put a bit aside each month for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds more like the world as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office folk who should worry, not us. A computer can't gather sheep off a hill in the fog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my work's safe for a while. The forms might get easier, if someone else does them. What I'd worry about is Callum, because his haulage firm already uses a computer to plan the routes, and the office staff who used to do that were let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Let Dad handle any new forms, or my cousin. Keep saving, keep the wedding. Wait and see what the big farms in the valley do with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Callum if his firm changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Callum there's always work on Ridge Farm, though it doesn't pay like driving. Callum would hate that, he likes his own wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said office folk should worry. Do you feel sorry for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do, a bit. My friend Shona works at the bank in town and she's already worried. But they chose a desk, we chose the hill.

say: I'd say **office folk** should worry, not hill farmers.
I'd note a computer **can't gather sheep** in the fog.
think: My **hill work** is safe for a while, and the forms might even get easier.
Callum's **haulage firm** already plans routes by computer and let its office staff go.
do: Let Dad or cousin Ewan **handle new forms**.
Keep saving and **keep the wedding** as planned.
**Wait and see** what valley farms do with robots.
S1.quote: A computer can't gather sheep off a hill in the fog.
fieldNote: She places the risk on **desk workers**, not on herself.
Her fiancé's firm is **already automating** the office side.
She offers Callum **farm work** but knows it won't suit him.

steps.text: Keep gathering and lambing the 400 ewes as usual
Watch the valley farms before trying any robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is dangerous and someone should stop it. Our MP should be fighting for farms, not letting tech companies run riot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be frightened. The thinking side, the forms and selling, goes in 2028, which is fine, but by 2031 the big farms would have robots shepherding, and our lamb price would drop through the floor. Callum's driving job would go with the robot lorries. We'd be newly married with nothing coming in but cheap lambs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the wedding forward to this spring and make it smaller, just the church and the hall. Callum would move onto Ridge Farm and we'd live in the old cottage rent-free. We'd save every penny for three years, and lean on family and the church if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray about it, and I'd not sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the gap before the robots help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us three years to save. But I don't know what we're saving for, if a robot can do my job and Callum's for less. That's what keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was no other way. I'd sooner go to my aunt in the village than the government. My family's never taken a handout.

say: I'd say this is **dangerous** and someone should stop it.
I'd demand our **MP** fight for farms, not tech companies.
think: By **2031** robot shepherds on big farms would crash lamb prices.
Callum's **driving job** would go with robot lorries.
do: Bring the **wedding forward** to spring and keep it small.
Move Callum into the **old cottage** rent-free on Ridge Farm.
Save every penny and lean on **family and church** if needed.
S2.quote: We'd be newly married with nothing coming in but cheap lambs.
fieldNote: She fears **two hits**: falling lamb prices and Callum's lost job.
The **three-year gap** feels like saving without a purpose.
She'd turn to **family** before any government help.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward to spring and hold it at the church hall
Move into the old Ridge Farm cottage rent-free with Callum
Ask the aunt in the village and the church for help if needed
Write to the MP asking for protection for hill farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better, but still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can't stop the world, but we can look after our own. I'd say farms like ours have survived worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives Callum time to find something else, maybe farm work on our place full-time. Robots around 2034 still worry me for the lamb price. I'd be 35, maybe with a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding next August as planned. Callum and I would save for three years, then he'd come onto the farm full-time around 2029. We'd keep the flock as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it feels like a worry, not a fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your future children about farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children the hill was here before the robots and the hill will be here after. Whether they farm it is up to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the flock as it is. Even if prices fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe cut to 350 ewes. But I won't sell the flock. They're hefted, which means they know their own patch of hill, and that takes generations.

say: I'd say we can't stop the world but can **look after our own**.
I'd remind people farms like ours have **survived worse**.
think: Five years lets **Callum** find other work, maybe on the farm.
Robots around **2034** still threaten lamb prices.
do: Keep the **wedding** next August as planned.
Bring Callum onto the **farm full-time** around 2029.
Cut to **350 ewes** if prices fall, but never sell.
feel: **Worried**, but as a worry rather than a **fear**.
S3.quote: I'd tell my children the hill was here before the robots and the hill will be here after.
fieldNote: Five years shifts her plan to bringing **Callum home** to the farm.
**Hefted** flocks (sheep that know their own hill) anchor her identity.
She expects **lamb prices** to fall but won't sell.

steps.text: Hold the wedding at St Michael's next August as planned
Bring Callum onto Ridge Farm full-time around 2029
Cut the flock to 350 ewes if lamb prices fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Dad would be 72.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and things will change before then. I'd not get worked up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets us get married, have children, and get Dad retired properly. By 2039 I'd be 40 and the farm would be mine. Robots might help with the hard bits, but I'd want people on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on farming. Save for the farmhouse roof. Callum keeps driving while he can and we plan for him to join the farm later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever buy a robot for the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day, if every other farm had one and the price came down. Something to carry the hay bales, perhaps. Not for the sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not for the sheep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the sheep know me and the dogs. A machine doesn't know when a ewe's about to go off and hide to lamb.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time** and much will change.
I'd **not get worked up** about it.
think: Ten years lets us **marry, have children** and retire Dad.
By **2039** the farm would be mine; I'd want people on the hill.
do: Carry on farming and **save for the roof**.
Keep Callum **driving** while he can, joining the farm later.
S4.quote: A machine doesn't know when a ewe's about to go off and hide to lamb.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **life plans** unfold in order.
She'd accept a robot for **hay bales**, never for the sheep.
She stays **uneasy** because Callum's driving still ends eventually.

steps.text: Save for the Ridge Farm farmhouse roof
Keep farming the ewes and cattle as now
Wait for robot prices to drop before buying a bale carrier

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Callum's job and our lamb price would go at the same time. What would help is fair prices for farmers, and stopping big companies from flooding the market. Not handouts, fair prices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. Bess and Moss work harder than any robot. A farm is a family, the dogs and sheep included, and nobody can put that on a screen.

headlineQuote: A farm is a family, the dogs and sheep included, and nobody can put that on a screen.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old **hill farmer** working Ridge Farm with her father.
She has **never used AI** and is proud of her notebook and pencil.
She is engaged to Callum, a **lorry driver**, with a wedding planned next August.
She's **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, fearing low lamb prices and Callum's job.
She prefers **family and church** to government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as Callum's job and lamb prices fall together.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair prices** for farmers and limits on big firms flooding the market.
